guide.title: TON address format explained
guide.description: How a TON address is built, and what the EQ, UQ, kQ and 0Q prefixes mean — with an example of every format.
guide.intro: Every account on The Open Network has a single identity but several valid text representations. This guide shows how a TON address is built, what the EQ, UQ, kQ and 0Q prefixes mean, and why the same wallet can look completely different depending on the format.

anatomy.title: What a TON address actually contains
anatomy.body: A TON address is a pair: a workchain ID that says which chain the account lives on, and a 256-bit account ID that identifies the contract on that chain. The masterchain is workchain -1, but nearly every wallet and token you will meet lives in the basechain, workchain 0.
anatomy.rawBody: The raw format writes that pair literally, as workchain:account_id with the account ID in lowercase hexadecimal. It carries no checksum and no network or bounceable flag, so it is used inside code, APIs and explorers rather than shared with people.
anatomy.friendlyBody: The user-friendly format packs the same account into 36 bytes and encodes them as 48 base64 characters. Those extra bytes are what make an address safe to copy and paste: a checksum catches typos, and a flag byte records the network and whether the address is bounceable.

meaning.flags: 0x11 for bounceable, 0x51 for non-bounceable; add 0x80 to mark the address testnet-only.
meaning.workchain: 0x00 for the basechain, 0xFF for the masterchain.
meaning.account: The 256-bit account ID — the same value as the hexadecimal half of the raw address.
meaning.checksum: CRC-16 over the previous 34 bytes. This is what makes a mistyped address fail instantly.

prefixes.title: What the EQ, UQ, kQ and 0Q prefixes mean
prefixes.body: The first two characters of a user-friendly address are a direct readout of the flag byte and the workchain, so you can tell the network and the bounceable setting at a glance — without decoding anything.

use.eq: Smart contracts and explorers — anything that should return funds if delivery fails.
use.uq: Wallets and exchange deposits. The safest default for simply receiving TON.
use.kq: Bounceable testnet address, used while developing and testing contracts.
use.zq: Non-bounceable testnet address, used for test wallets.
use.ef: Masterchain bounceable — validators and system contracts.
use.uf: Masterchain non-bounceable — rarely seen outside infrastructure.

encoding.title: Encoding rules worth knowing
items: A user-friendly TON address is always exactly 48 characters. If yours is shorter or longer, it is not a valid TON address.
Base64 is case-sensitive. EQCD… and eqcd… are different strings, and only the exact casing passes validation.
Two alphabets are in circulation: standard base64 uses + and /, while URL-safe base64 replaces them with - and _. Both decode to the same account, and TON tooling prefers the URL-safe form.
The raw format has no checksum, so nothing catches a typo for you. Always verify a raw address before sending funds.

items.q: My wallet shows UQ but the explorer shows EQ
items.a: Both are the same account. Explorers usually display the bounceable EQ form while wallets show the non-bounceable UQ form for deposits. Convert either one and compare the raw addresses to confirm they match.

items.q: An exchange rejected my TON address
items.a: Most exchanges expect the mainnet non-bounceable UQ form for deposits. A bounceable EQ address can cause the transfer to be returned if the receiving contract has not been deployed yet.

items.q: Why does my testnet address not work on mainnet?
items.a: A kQ or 0Q address has the testnet-only flag set, so mainnet wallets refuse it. The underlying account ID is identical — convert it to the EQ or UQ form to use the same account on mainnet.

items.q: Is a Telegram wallet address a TON address?
items.a: Yes. Telegram Wallet, Tonkeeper and other TON wallets all use the same address format; only the display form differs between apps.

A TON address identifies a wallet or smart contract on The Open Network. It combines a workchain ID with a 256-bit account ID and can be shown in several equivalent formats — raw and user-friendly (bounceable or non-bounceable).

items.q: What is the difference between bounceable and non-bounceable addresses?
items.a: A bounceable address (prefix EQ) returns the funds if the destination contract cannot process the message, so it is used for smart contracts. A non-bounceable address (prefix UQ) does not return funds and is typically used for wallets and exchange deposits.

items.q: What is a raw TON address?
items.a: The raw format is the low-level representation written as workchain:hex, for example 0:83dfd552e63729b472fcbcc8c45ebcc6691702558b68ec7527e1ba403a0f31a8. It is a 32-byte hash with an 8-bit workchain ID and is used programmatically rather than shared with users.

items.q: What is a normalized TON address?
items.a: A normalized address is the canonical user-friendly form (URL-safe base64 with the bounceable flag off). Normalizing lets you reliably compare or deduplicate addresses that point to the same account.

items.q: What do the EQ and UQ prefixes mean?
items.a: In user-friendly base64 addresses, EQ marks a mainnet bounceable address and UQ marks a mainnet non-bounceable address. Both encode the same account and differ only by the bounceable flag.

items.q: What do the kQ and 0Q prefixes mean?
items.a: They are the testnet counterparts of EQ and UQ: kQ is a bounceable testnet address and 0Q is a non-bounceable testnet address. Only the testnet-only bit in the flag byte is set, so the underlying account is the same.

items.q: How long is a TON address?
items.a: A user-friendly TON address is exactly 48 base64 characters. A raw address is the workchain ID, a colon, and 64 hexadecimal characters — for example 0: followed by the 32-byte account ID.

Yes. User-friendly addresses are base64, so upper- and lower-case letters are different characters. Copy addresses instead of retyping them and rely on the built-in checksum — TONify flags any address that fails it.

items.q: How do I convert a TON address?
items.a: Paste it into the field above. TONify detects the format automatically, accepts raw, bounceable, non-bounceable and testnet input, and shows every equivalent form at once. You can paste several addresses together and export the result as CSV.

items.a: Yes. TONify is a free, open-source tool and all conversion happens locally in your browser — the addresses you paste are never sent to any server.
